title: Sources for the perturbation laws (lean/Delphi/Perturb.lean)
fetchedVia: Europe PMC REST: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?format=json&resultType=core&query=EXT_ID:<pmid>%20AND%20SRC:MED (abstracts); https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/<pmcid>/fullTextXML (full text, where quoted from the body)
rule: Every empirical constant used by Perturb.lean, by its non-vacuity witness, or by the browser-check perturbation rows is listed here with the sentence it comes from. A constant marked kind 'physical-standard' is a defined physical constant, not fetched from Europe PMC, and is said so. No Aves data. Design inputs (drag coefficient, reference area, U_crit of a designed animal, assimilation efficiency, costs) are committed by the design and never defaulted here.

schulte2015.title: The effects of temperature on aerobic metabolism: towards a mechanistic understanding of the responses of ectotherms to a changing environment
schulte2015.quote: As temperature increases, the rate of metabolism increases and then rapidly declines at higher temperatures - a response that can be described using a thermal performance curve (TPC).
schulte2015.usedFor: the thermal-window hypothesis (ThermalPerformance.zero_outside): performance bounded by a curve that falls to zero outside [CTmin, CTmax]

rome1992b.authors: Rome LC, Sosnicki A, Choi IH
rome1992b.title: The influence of temperature on muscle function in the fast swimming scup. II. The mechanics of red muscle.
rome1992b.quote: The maximal power generation was correspondingly about 50% greater in scup than in carp (71 W kg-1 at 10 degrees C and 134 W kg-1 at 20 degrees C; Q10 = 1.88).
rome1992b.usedFor: Q10 1.88, P_ref 134 W/kg at T_ref 20 C, and the measured interval [10, 20] C of the witness (scupSustained)

rome1992a.authors: Rome LC, Choi IH, Lutz G, Sosnicki A
rome1992a.title: The influence of temperature on muscle function in the fast swimming scup. I. Shortening velocity and muscle recruitment
rome1992a.quote: at 10 degrees C, the scup could swim to only 54 cm s-1 before recruiting their white muscle whereas, at 20 degrees C, they could swim to 80 cm s-1.
rome1992a.usedFor: U_crit 0.80 m/s of the witness (sustained, red-muscle-only top speed at 20 C); also shows the sustained speed itself falls with temperature (0.54 m/s at 10 C)

romeswank1992.title: The influence of temperature on power output of scup red muscle during cyclical length changes.
romeswank1992.quote: maximum power was 27.9 W kg-1 at 20 degrees C and 12.8 W kg-1 at 10 degrees C, giving a Q10 of 2.29
romeswank1992.usedFor: a second Q10 for power (2.29, work-loop), recorded to show the Q10 is a measured, method-dependent number (1.88 steady vs 2.29 cyclic); not used in a proof

morgan2018.authors: Morgan R, Finnøen MH, Jutfelt F
morgan2018.title: CTmax is repeatable and doesn't reduce growth in zebrafish.
morgan2018.quote: CT max also increased from the first (40.97 ± 0.10 °C) to the second trial (+0.30 ± 0.10 °C ...)
morgan2018.usedFor: reference CTmax of zebrafish (40.97 C, naive fish, ramp 0.3 C/min), recorded for the Studio as a reference value only; the checker never defaults a CTmax. No CTmin was fetched.

plaut2001.journal: Comp Biochem Physiol A Mol Integr Physiol
plaut2001.title: Critical swimming speed: its ecological relevance.
plaut2001.quote: Fishes tend to maintain their position in the water tunnel against the current until fatigue sets in. The time and velocity at which the fish fatigue are used to calculate the critical swimming speed.
plaut2001.usedFor: the station-holding definition of U_crit (sustained swimming speed at most U_crit; holding position means ground speed U_swim - U_current >= 0)

yancey2020.journal: J Exp Zool A Ecol Integr Physiol
yancey2020.title: Cellular responses in marine animals to hydrostatic pressure.
yancey2020.quote: Hydrostatic pressure (HP), increasing by 1 atm per 10 m in the ocean ... The key example is the osmolyte trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), which marine fishes and crustaceans accumulates linearly with depth.
yancey2020.usedFor: Hydrostatic witness p0 = 1 atm, k = 0.1 atm/m; water density of the swim witness 10132.5/9.80665 = 1033 kg/m^3 (derived from 1 atm per 10 m and g0, so approximate); linear TMAO with depth

kerr2023.authors: Kerr JR, White PR, Leighton TG, Silva LGM, Kemp PS
kerr2023.title: Boyle's Law ignores dynamic processes in governing barotrauma in fish.
kerr2023.quote: The expansion and potential rupture of the swim bladder due to rapid decompression ... is generally assumed to be governed by Boyle's Law ... these conditions include ... (1) when rate of pressure change is anything but very slow compared to the resonant frequency of the swim bladder
kerr2023.usedFor: Boyle's law for the swim bladder and its stated limit: quasi-static pressure change only

yancey2014.authors: Yancey PH, Gerringer ME, Drazen JC, Rowden AA, Jamieson A
yancey2014.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
yancey2014.title: Marine fish may be biochemically constrained from inhabiting the deepest ocean depths.
yancey2014.quote: TMAO accumulation with depth results in increasing internal osmolality (typically 350 mOsmol/kg in shallow species compared with seawater's 1,100 mOsmol/kg) ... We found their muscles to have a TMAO content of 386 ± 18 mmol/kg and osmolality of 991 ± 22 mOsmol/kg. These data fit previous extrapolations and, combined with new osmolalities from bathyal and abyssal fishes, predict isosmotic state at 8,200 m.
yancey2014.usedFor: OsmolyteDepthCap: cap 8200 m; witness a = 350, osmolality 991 at 7000 m (b = 641/7000 per m), seawater 1100; the two-point line meets seawater at 8190 m

narayanan2022.title: Enhanced Vertical Navigation Using Barometric Measurements.
narayanan2022.quote: p(h) = p0 (1 - beta (h - h0)/T0)^(g0/(R_d beta)) ... The nominal atmosphere is usually characterized by a temperature lapse rate of 6.5 K/km ... Utilizing the ISA for the reference atmospheric values (pressure: 1013.25 hPa, temperature: 288.15 K)
narayanan2022.usedFor: ISATroposphere form; T0 = 288.15 K, beta = 0.0065 K/m, p0 = 1013.25 hPa

bihun2024.authors: Bihun CJ, Stewart EMC, Lechner ER, Brownscombe JW, Raby GD
bihun2024.title: Thermal performance curves for aerobic scope and specific dynamic action in a sexually dimorphic piscivore: implications for a warming climate.
bihun2024.quote: The proportion of digestible energy lost to SDA (i.e. the SDA coefficient) was consistent at 6% and was unrelated to temperature, body mass, sex or ration size.
bihun2024.usedFor: SDACoefficient witness s = 0.06 (fraction of DIGESTIBLE energy, the base Perturb.lean uses)

mcleodclark2016.title: Limited Capacity for Faster Digestion in Larval Coral Reef Fish at an Elevated Temperature.
mcleodclark2016.quote: the percent of total meal energy used for SDA (SDA coefficient: 10.1±1.3% vs. 13.0±1.7%)
mcleodclark2016.usedFor: a LARVAL-stage SDA coefficient (Amphiprion percula, 28.5 vs 31.5 C), recorded for the developmental-stage axis; note its base is TOTAL meal energy, not digestible energy, so it is not interchangeable with bihun2024 without an assimilation efficiency

secor2009.title: Specific dynamic action: a review of the postprandial metabolic response.
secor2009.quote: The average maximum increase in metabolic rate stemming from digestion ranges from a modest 25% for humans to 136% for fishes
secor2009.usedFor: the SDA term of the energy budget (definition); 136% peak increase recorded, not used in a proof

savagewest2007.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
savagewest2007.title: A quantitative, theoretical framework for understanding mammalian sleep.
savagewest2007.quote: Here, we develop a general, quantitative theory for mammalian sleep that relates many of its fundamental parameters to metabolic rate and body size ... Data for 96 species of mammals
savagewest2007.usedFor: the reason NO sleep law is formalised: the only quantitative sleep theory fetched is for mammals; none was found for teleosts

jamieson2026.authors: Jamieson AJ, Swanborn DJB, Bond T, Cundy MC, Fujiwara Y, Lindsay D, Stott MS, Kitazato H
jamieson2026.title: Faunal biodiversity of the lower abyssal and hadal zones of the Japan, Ryukyu and Izu-Ogasawara trenches (NW Pacific Ocean; 4534-9775 m).
jamieson2026.quote: Their depth ranges were 6023-8336 m, 6579-7621 m and 6860-8022 m, respectively. Pseudoliparis sp. indet. 1 at 8336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench is the deepest recorded fish ( Jamieson et al. 2023b ).
jamieson2026.primary: Jamieson AJ, Maroni PJ, Bond T, Niyazi Y, Kolbusz J, Arasu P, Kitazato H 2023, New maximum depth record for bony fish: Teleostei, Scorpaeniformes, Liparidae (8336 m, Izu-Ogasawara Trench), Deep-Sea Research I 199:104132, doi:10.1016/j.dsr.2023.104132 (not indexed in Europe PMC; the 8336 m figure is taken from the 2026 paper quoting it)
jamieson2026.usedFor: CONTRADICTS the osmolyte depth cap: a teleost observed (video, baited lander) 136 m below the 8200 m cap and 146 m below the witness crossing of 8190 m. The cap is therefore a soft limit, not a hard one; P3b is contested.
jamieson2026.flaggedBy: sim-engine/scenarios/ENVIRONMENT.md (environment scenario thread), checked here against the source

notFormalised.reason: No quantitative sleep law for a teleost was found. The only quantitative theory fetched (savagewest2007) is built and tested on 96 mammal species; applying it to a fish would be an invented law. No Lean row; the Studio must show sleep as unconstrained by Lean.
No quantitative law fetched; photoperiod is held at average in conditions/baseline.json. No Lean row.
No source fetched for a grip or attachment law; not formalised.
Burst (anaerobic) performance is outside every bound here; the Fick and Q10 bounds are for SUSTAINED power. Not formalised.
No fetched source gave an energy assimilation efficiency for a teleost; the design must commit it (P5 cannot evaluate without it).
No CTmin was fetched; the design must commit its window (P1 cannot evaluate without it).

claims.label: Thermal window and Q10: no sustained power outside [CTmin, CTmax], at most P_ref Q10^((T-T_ref)/10) inside
claims.statement: If sustained power is zero outside the thermal window and at most the Q10-scaled reference inside it, then at every temperature the sustained power is at most P_ref Q10^((T - T_ref)/10), and outside the window no positive power is sustained.
claims.notation: P <= sustained(T) implies P <= P_ref Q10^((T - T_ref)/10); T outside [CTmin, CTmax] implies P <= 0
kernelChecked: The Q10 bound at every temperature, inside or outside the window.
No positive sustained power outside the window.
Non-vacuity: the scup numbers (Q10 1.88, 134 W/kg at 20 C, measured on [10, 20] C) satisfy the hypothesis.
assumed: The thermal performance curve is zero outside [CTmin, CTmax] (Schulte 2015 describes the shape; the window of a designed animal is a design input).
The Q10 rule inside the window, with one Q10 for the whole window; Q10 is method-dependent (1.88 steady, 2.29 work-loop for the same muscle).
Body temperature equals water temperature (ectotherm), as conditions/baseline.json states.

claims.label: No design holds station in a current above U_crit, or above the speed its aerobic supply can pay drag for
claims.statement: With ground speed U_swim - U_current not negative, sustained swimming at most U_crit, drag power rho C_d A U^3 / 2 paid by a sustained power that is aerobic (Fick), the current satisfies U_current <= U_crit and rho C_d A U_current^3 / 2 <= eta E Q Ca.
claims.notation: U_current <= U_crit and rho Cd A U_current^3 / 2 <= eta E Q Ca
kernelChecked: Both necessary conditions for holding station, composed with the Fick bound of lean/Delphi/Flight.lean.
Non-vacuity with U_crit 0.80 m/s (scup, red muscle, 20 C).
assumed: Steady swimming, quadratic drag with a constant C_d (a design input), drag area A (a design input).
Sustained swimming is aerobic; burst-and-coast and anaerobic sprinting are outside the bound.
U_crit as defined by the incremental-velocity protocol (Plaut 2001).

claims.label: Boyle's law for a closed swim bladder: volume at depth is the surface volume times p0 / P(d)
claims.statement: With absolute pressure p0 + k d and P(d) V(d) constant at every depth, V(d) = V(0) p0 / P(d); the volume falls with depth, and keeping the volume needs gas in proportion 1 + k d / p0.
kernelChecked: The Boyle volume, its monotone decrease with depth, the secretion ratio.
assumed: Ideal gas, fixed amount and temperature, quasi-static pressure change (Kerr et al. 2023: fails for fast decompression).
Bladder wall compliance ignored (gas pressure equals ambient).

claims.label: Osmolyte depth cap (CONTESTED): no teleost below 8200 m if it cannot be hyperosmotic to seawater; a fish has been recorded at 8336 m
claims.statement: If internal osmolality rises linearly with depth (TMAO), the isosmotic depth is at most 8200 m, and a teleost cannot be hyperosmotic to seawater, then no teleost lives below 8200 m.
claims.notation: osm(d) = a + b d <= sw and (sw - a)/b <= 8200 imply d <= 8200
kernelChecked: The depth bound from the linear osmolality and the no-reversal hypothesis.
Non-vacuity: 350 mOsmol/kg shallow, 991 at 7000 m, seawater 1100 give 8190 m, inside the published 8200 m.
assumed: Yancey et al. 2014's hypothesis that greater depths would require reversal of osmotic gradients; it is a prediction from extrapolation, not an observed limit (no fish has been found below 8400 m).
Linear osmolality in depth; teleosts only (not elasmobranchs or invertebrates).

CONTRADICTED BY OBSERVATION: a teleost (Pseudoliparis sp.) has been recorded at 8336 m (Jamieson et al. 2026, quoting Jamieson et al. 2023), below the 8200 m cap. Either the isosmotic depth is deeper than predicted for that species or the no-reversal premise fails; the crossing is a soft limit.

contradictedBy.observation: Pseudoliparis sp. indet. 1 filmed at 8336 m, Izu-Ogasawara Trench
contradictedBy.consequence: The theorem is correct under its hypotheses, but the hypothesis OsmolyteDepthCap (isosmotic depth at most 8200 m, no reversal of the osmotic gradient) is false of at least one real teleost. The osmolyte crossing is a soft limit (an approximate ceiling, within about 2%), not a cap.

claims.label: Altitude and wind: v_min proportional to 1/sqrt(rho) with rho from the ISA troposphere; glide ground range (L/D) h (1 + w/u), w positive for a tailwind
claims.statement: In the barometric troposphere rho(h) = rho0 (1 - beta h/T0)^n density falls with height, v_min = sqrt(2W/(S C_L,max))/sqrt(rho) so the ratio of minimum speeds is sqrt(rho1/rho2), and v_min rises with height. A steady glide with horizontal airspeed u, sink s and along-track wind w (positive tailwind) covers (u/s) h (1 + w/u), at most (L/D)max h (1 + w/u) when w >= -u.
kernelChecked: ISA density monotone in the troposphere; v_min inverse-square-root in density; the glide ground range identity and bound with the stated sign convention.
assumed: The barometric (ISA) form with a constant lapse rate, valid below the tropopause (about 11 km); real atmospheres deviate (Narayanan and Osechas 2022).
Steady glide, constant wind, no updraft (a vertical wind component is not modelled).

claims.label: Daily energy balance: a I (1 - s) < R + Act means mass declines; holding mass needs I >= (R + Act)/(a (1 - s))
claims.statement: Under energy conservation over a day, eps dm = a I - (R + Act + s a I) with SDA a fraction s of the digestible energy, a deficit a I (1 - s) < R + Act forces dm < 0, and holding or gaining mass needs intake at least (R + Act)/(a (1 - s)).
claims.notation: eps dm = a I (1 - s) - (R + Act)
kernelChecked: Mass decline under a deficit; the minimum intake; non-vacuity with s = 0.06 (walleye).
assumed: Energy conservation with every cost listed (routine, activity, SDA) and no unlisted loss; excretory losses are inside the assimilation efficiency a.
SDA proportional to digestible intake (Bihun et al. 2024 found the coefficient constant across temperature, mass and ration).
